newsitem.title: GERMANY: German nuclear waste convoy leaves for dump.
newsitem.headline: German nuclear waste convoy leaves for dump.

text.p: A controversial nuclear waste shipment set off for the last leg of its journey on Wednesday to a dump in northern Germany, amid massive protests by hundreds of anti-nuclear activists.
Six flat-bed trucks carrying containers of spent fuel rods left a loading station in the town of Dannenberg under heavy police escort for the 20-km (14-mile) journey to the Gorleben storage depot.
The first truck left the gates and ground to a halt outside, where a thick cordon of riot police were gathered to prevent protesters blocking the road.

But after a few minutes it moved on, followed by the other five trucks which made their way slowly towards the convoy's final destination to loud booing and whistling from hundreds of protesters pressed back from the road by police lines.
Only a short distance further along the possible route to Gorleben protesters had chained themselves to a rope that was tied to trees on either side of the road, blocking the way.
About 5,000 demonstrators were also posted along roads leading to the dump to block the way.

Germany's biggest post-war security operation, which has involved 30,000 police nationwide to protect the radioactive shipment, reached its climax as police tried to clear the route from the station to the nuclear waste depot.

Police said militant demonstrators fired flare pistols and pelted riot police with stones. Officers turned water cannon on them at one place in the countryside along the route after the convoy started to roll.
Border guards in helicopters flew over the area, which was beginning to look as though it had been hit by civil war.
Explosives experts were called to one place where an anonymous caller said a bomb had been planted. It was not yet clear whether the object was an explosive device or a dummy.
Earlier, police turned water cannon from three trucks on hundreds of protesters to clear them from the gates of the loading station in Dannenberg.
Using low pressure bursts of water designed mainly to weaken their resolve and make them uncomfortable, the police continued spraying the seated demonstrators for about three hours.

Many drenched demonstrators, who tried to protect themselves with sheets of plastic and raincoats, went to the side of the road to change into dry clothing provided by other activists and returned to the street.
Police warned the activists by loudspeaker that the drenching would continue unless they stopped their sit-down blockade.
The nuclear waste shipment arrived at Dannenberg in six sealed containers on a 500-metre long train from southern Germany early on Tuesday.

Activists have already tried to make the roads to Gorleben unusable by damaging the surface of some, tunnelling underneath others, while local farmers have set up barricades with tractors and haystacks.
On Tuesday hundreds of masked militants lobbed petrol bombs and pelted police with stones to protest against the shipment.
Two police officers were injured in the clashes and a thick cordon of police encircled about 250 demonstrators to take their fingerprints and personal details.
